meta.description: No — Wayne Dyer didn't coin it. It's an anonymous modern proverb attested by 1953; Dyer used only a paraphrase in 2009. Here's the paper trail.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'This is your life, not a dress rehearsal'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Wayne Dyer. It's an anonymous saying attested by 1953, origin untraceable per Quote Investigator; Dyer only paraphrased it in 2009.

answer.label: Not Wayne Dyer — an anonymous modern proverb
answer.sourceLine: This is a floating modern proverb with no identifiable author. Quote Investigator ↗ traces it to at least 1953 and concludes the origin is untraceable, recommending the label “Anonymous.” Dyer used only a loose variant — “Somehow we’ve got this notion that life is a dress rehearsal. It isn’t” — in a 2009 book, long after the saying was already in wide circulation, and never in this exact wording.

source.excerpt: “This is your life, not a dress rehearsal.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ locates the earliest instance in 1953 — Pastor Lawrence T. Holman of the Church of the Nazarene used it as an evening-sermon title in the Covina Argus-Citizen — and judges the origin “probably untraceable.”

The same investigation records the phrase spreading through a 1972 Big Sky resort ad linked to broadcaster Chet Huntley, Sydney Omarr’s 1976 astrology column, actress Katharine Ross in 1977, and Judith Michaels t-shirts in 1977, per Quote Investigator ↗.

Wayne Dyer’s appearance is late and loose: his 2009 book Staying on the Path reads “we’ve got this notion that life is a dress rehearsal. It isn’t,” not the popular slogan, again per Quote Investigator ↗.
source.excerptNote: The exact phrase appeared on Judith Michaels designer t-shirts by 1977. Dyer’s nearest version reads: “Somehow we’ve got this notion that life is a dress rehearsal. It isn’t. This is it!”

source.rightsNote: The exact wording is an anonymous modern proverb with no identifiable first-publication work — Quote Investigator ↗ deems its origin untraceable — so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted for the phrase itself. Individual later texts that use it (e.g., Wayne Dyer’s 2009 book, or Jim Donovan’s book of the same title) carry their own separate copyrights.

author.name: Wayne Dyer
author.heading: About the man it’s pinned on
author.bio: Wayne W. Dyer was an American self-help author and speaker whose 1976 bestseller Your Erroneous Zones made him a household name in the personal-development world. Because his upbeat, aphoristic style is endlessly quotable, feel-good lines are routinely pinned on him — but this particular proverb was circulating for decades before he ever used a paraphrase of it, and he never coined the popular wording.

misattribution.heading: So who really said it?
misattribution.intro: A punchy, life-affirming slogan with no known author is exactly the kind of line that gets adopted by whichever famous motivator is quotable this decade. Wayne Dyer is the current magnet, but he’s far from the first mouth it passed through.

items.why: Dyer’s only documented use is a loose variant in his 2009 book Staying on the Path — “we’ve got this notion that life is a dress rehearsal. It isn’t” — decades after the saying was already on t-shirts and in newspapers, per Quote Investigator ↗.

items.who: Chet Huntley, Katharine Ross, Sydney Omarr, Drake
items.why: A 1972 Big Sky resort ad tied to broadcaster Chet Huntley, a 1976 Sydney Omarr column, actress Katharine Ross in 1977, and rapper Drake in 2010 all used versions — none originated it, again per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest attribution is Anonymous: the earliest known instance is a 1953 sermon title, and Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the true origin is untraceable.

context.heading: Why it sticks
lead: The saying works as a compact memento vivere — a reminder that there is no do-over, so live now. That universality is exactly why it has no single owner: it reads as folk wisdom, and folk wisdom accretes famous names rather than keeping the real one.

By the mid-1970s it was already free-floating culture — graffiti, gossip columns, slogan t-shirts — which is the surest sign a line has outrun any individual author well before the self-help era claimed it.
context.pull: A slogan on a 1977 t-shirt is not a quotation with an author — it’s a proverb.
